text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday cleared the $20 billion merger between British Telecommunications and MCI Communications Corp of the United States after the companies made several concessions.
The concessions would prevent the partners dominating telephone services between Britain and the United States, and the British audioconferencing market, it said in a statement.
"The Commission has considered that the undertakings proposed by the parties during the proceedings are sufficient to address the competition concerns," the statement said.

The merger will give BT control of MCI, in which it already owns 20 percent, to create the world's second largest telecoms group based on market capitalisation after Japan's NTT Corp and neck-and-neck with U.S. long-distance calls leader AT&T Corp.
In London a BT spokesman welcomed the decision. "We're very pleased. They placed a couple of conditions on clearance and we were only too happy to agree to them," he told Reuters.

EU regulatory approval had never been a problem as the British telecoms market is one of the most liberalised in the 15-nation European Union and both partners agreed to cooperate with the Commission.
The deal still faces its main test in the United States where the green light hinges on whether Britain is deemed to be as open to fair competition as the American market.
BT expects to win U.S. blessing for its deal with the country's second biggest long-distance carrier by the autumn.
The companies made the following concessions in Europe:
-- To make available capacity from the companies' transatlantic cable to British operators, without delay and at prices corresponding to BT's "true cost of purchasing".

The Commission said this was justified by the "current capacity shortage" on existing international transmission facilities and the fact that satellite does not yet provide a "satisfactory substitute" for submarine cable in the supply of transatlantic phone calls.
-- To sell BT's capacity currently leased to other operators on the Britain-U.S. route if they requested it and on fair terms.

-- To sell to other operators, at their request and without delay, circuits owned by BT in Britain thus enabling them to provide voice telephone services on the Britain-U.S. route "on an end-to-end basis".
-- To arrange for the divestiture of MCI's audioconferencing business in Britain.

The Commission said that together the two companies would have controlled 80 percent of the British market for telephone conferences. Their entrenched position would have made entrance of new rivals difficult despite the low investments needed to set up a new business.
